title: Chapter 9: On the Bosporus (p. 46–60)

Journey · Children’s Books

Chapter 9: On the Bosporus (p. 46–60)

Pages 46–60 (15 pages)
Page 46

Chapter 9: On the Bosporus “Acharn Sujin explained about Buddhism to our guide in Turkey, Ms. Tuna, while we were having a tour on the Bosporus river.” The guide. Nina writes: “Acharn Sujin explained about Buddhism to our guide in Turkey, Ms. Tuna, while we were having a tour on the Bosporus river.” The Bosporus is the water that runs through Istanbul. Ms Tuna belonged to another religion. She said: “I am a Moslem, I believe in God. When I am in a very bad mood I pray to Him and then I feel better.” Acharn Sujin did not ask her to give up her faith. She asked her about things that anybody can know right now. Feelings. Acharn began with feeling, because everybody has it: “We would like to have pleasant feeling all the time, but this is not possible. If we can understand the causes of our different feelings it will help us to have less unpleasant feeling. Life is so uncontrollable because each moment is conditioned1.” And: “In order to understand our life from moment to moment we do not have to think in terms of a particular religion. Realities2 such as seeing, hearing or feeling are true for everybody, no matter which language we use in order to name them. Don’t we all have pleasant and unpleasant feelings? Can you control your feelings?” Rich and poor. Ms Tuna said that some people work hard and never become rich, while others have everything without working; in Arabic this is called “kismet3“, destiny. Acharn asked: “Can the poor be happy and the rich be unhappy?” Ms Tuna agreed: “There are very rich people who are not happy and there are poor people who are very happy; they are rich in heart. They do not attach importance to material4 things.” Acharn asked: “Is happiness caused by God or by yourself? Do you have the ability to condition5 your own feelings?” Ms Tuna said: “Yes, I can.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 46

Page 47

Where is the soul when one sleeps? Ms Tuna said that the soul never dies: “We think that the soul is in the body. When one dies, the soul goes away.” Acharn asked: “When one is sleeping where is the soul?” Ms Tuna did not know. Acharn went on, one question at a time. In the morning there is seeing. “Is it the soul which sees?” Ms Tuna thought so. “At the moment of hearing, is it the soul which hears?” “Sure.” Then Acharn summed up: “So, the soul has many functions6 in a day. Seeing is one function, hearing is another function. Besides these, there are the functions of smelling, tasting, touching and thinking. I believe that the soul sleeps too.” what Ms Tuna called the soul one thing? seeing hearing smelling tasting touching thinking dreaming sleeping “I think that seeing is different from hearing. Seeing and hearing occur at different moments and experience different objects.” “So, the soul has many functions in a day. Seeing is one function, hearing is another function.” Ms Tuna asked about dreams. Acharn: “Everyone dreams. So, the soul is dreaming. The body cannot dream.” She agreed that what sees, hears and dreams is not the body: “The body cannot see, but the soul is seeing. The body cannot think, but the soul is thinking.” Then she asked: “How many souls do you have?” Ms Tuna: “Only one, of course.” Acharn: “I think that seeing is different from hearing. Seeing and hearing occur at different moments and experience7 different objects8.” Ms Tuna said: “All this is deep in meaning, difficult to understand. It is beyond my thinking.” Light and darkness. Acharn explained why she kept to what can be experienced: “It is beneficial9 to talk about what we can experience right now because we can understand that. When we talk about what we cannot experience directly we are in darkness. When we understand the characteristics10 and functions of the realities which can be directly experienced there is light. I would like to understand more and more the realities of my life.” Ms Tuna said that to be happy one should be a good Muslim: pray, read the Quran, keep the fast of Ramadan, and give money to the poor. Acharn did not argue. She spoke about wisdom: “Ignorance11 is the opposite of wisdom or understanding. Wisdom is to be considered more valuable than any kind of property; it is the most beneficial thing in life. I think that wisdom can develop.” Ms Tuna said: “I agree with you.” Consciousness instead of soul. Acharn Sujin said why she preferred another word: A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 47

Page 48

“I think that there are many different kinds of consciousness12. We can use the word consciousness instead of soul. The word soul can give rise to misunderstandings, it is not precise enough. If we use the word soul it implies something permanent. Consciousness experiences one object at a time and it is not permanent; it changes all the time.” Seeing is one kind of consciousness. “Seeing is seeing for everyone, it does not belong to any race or nationality. Also animals see. Seeing is the same no matter what you call it. Thus, it is an absolute13 truth for everyone, it is an absolute or ultimate14 reality.” And she asked Ms Tuna: “Can you touch visible object? Do you see me? You can only see visible object.” A person is thought of after seeing: “A person cannot be seen, there can only be thinking about a person.” Why are people different? Ms Tuna asked why people have different characters from birth. Her mother cared for everybody, while some people never want to help anyone. Acharn answered: “People are different, they do not have wholesome15 moments all the time. There are wholesome realities and unwholesome16 realities. Kindness and compassion17 are wholesome, cruelty, hatred and jealousy are unwholesome. There are for everybody conditions for wholesome moments as well as for unwholesome moments. The arising18 of wholesomeness or unwholesomeness depends on what has been accumulated19.” To become a good person, Acharn said, “you have to develop wholesomeness, you have to train yourself. Just as when you want to be skillful20 in cooking you have to train yourself so that one day you will be a good cook.” “Just as when you want to be skillful in cooking you have to train yourself so that one day you will be a good cook.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 48

Page 49

Ms Tuna said that some people do not want to be good. Acharn: “You can help them to understand the benefit of being wholesome so that they will be kind to others.” And: “If you are friendly to others they will be friendly to you. If you do not like other people they will not like you.” One moment, then gone. Acharn ended with words for people of any religion: “Religion is only a term which stands for what one believes in. But if we don’t label anything we can understand realities as they are. We can understand realities which are true for everybody, no matter what religion he professes21, no matter what nationality he is.” “Life goes on from moment to moment, until death. Life is only one moment of experiencing an object and then it is gone, forever.” HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 2. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 3. destiny: what is said to be fixed to happen to someone 4. material: made of matter; the stuff that does not know anything 5. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 6. function: the job that something does 7. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 8. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 9. beneficial: helpful; good for someone 10. characteristic: the mark by which something is known; what is special about it 11. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 12. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 13. absolute: complete and real in itself; not depending on names or ideas 14. ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away 15. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 16. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 17. compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering 18. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 19. accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it 20. skilful: done well, with skill; here, good for the mind (unskilful: bad for the mind) 21. profess: to say openly that one belongs to a religion A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 49

Page 50

Chapter 10: Questions on the plane “They interviewed each other while on the plane and this resulted in a combination of questions and answers from the three of them.” Nina writes: “What follows is an interview between Gabi, Alan and Nina, while travelling in Egypt together with Acharn Sujin. They interviewed each other while on the plane and this resulted in a combination of questions and answers from the three of them.” The questions are the kind anyone might ask who has just heard of the Buddha’s teaching. The answers are the three friends’ own. Is Buddhism different? What does the Buddha’s teaching have that is found nowhere else? “Through Buddhism we learn to understand realities1 which can be directly experienced2. Buddhism does not teach particular concepts3 we have to believe in, but it teaches the development of understanding of all realities within and around ourselves. Thus, we can verify4 the truth.” Does a Buddhist have to have faith, then? “We don’t have to follow the Buddha’s teachings blindly. We learn what he teaches and then we have to verify it ourselves”. “I am quite happy.” One of them said that he was quite happy and had few problems, so why would anyone need Buddhism? The answer: “I am not satisfied with the explanations about life which are given by science, biology or chemistry. Through Buddhism I learn what life really is: one moment of experiencing an object5.” And when a person looks closely at these moments, “one realizes one’s faults and vices6“. Defilements. What are defilements7? “These are unwholesome8 states of mind which are not beneficial9. They cause harm to us or to others sooner or later. Hatred, for example, is an unskillful10 state of mind. When hatred arises11 we harm ourselves and others. At such moments there is no peace of mind.” And: “When people become angry, they are inclined12 to do something they may regret later on.” Rightful anger? History books say that kings had rightful13 anger. Is there such a thing? A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 50

Page 51

“Anger is always unwholesome, no matter what the cause is. It harms yourself and others. This does not mean that you cannot be firm with others when it is necessary for people’s benefit, but hatred and anger are always unwholesome. At such moments you have no balance of mind, you are not sane14.” Three roots. Are there other defilements besides anger? “There are many kinds of defilements. Three basic defilements are roots for unwholesome states of mind, namely: attachment15, anger or aversion16, and ignorance17.” These are lobha (attachment), dosa (aversion) and moha (ignorance), named in Chapter 2. unwholesome states of mind hatred, jealousy, greed, moodiness, cruelty ... lobha attachment dosa aversion moha ignorance “Ignorance conditions all defilements. There is ignorance with each unwholesome moment of consciousness.” “Three basic defilements are roots for unwholesome states of mind, namely: attachment, anger or aversion, and ignorance.” Love. Is love wholesome18 or unwholesome? The one word stands for two different realities: “Love can represent the reality which is kindness towards other people. It arises when we consider their welfare. However, love can also represent an unwholesome reality. When we are attached to a person we actually think of ourselves and that is an unwholesome reality. When we have to be separated from that person, attachment conditions19 aversion and displeasure. When unselfish20 loving-kindness21 arises you don’t think of your own pleasure.” Should there be no attachment between husband and wife, or parents and children? “It is not a matter of should or should not. You are as you are. However, there can be a more precise understanding of what is unselfish love, or true considerateness22 for others and what is attachment, selfish love.” The difference: “Unselfish love is characterised by considering the welfare of others. Attachment to other people is for the sake of one’s own pleasant feeling.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 51

Page 52

the word “love” unselfish love kindness, mettā (loving-kindness): kusala (wholesome) “considering the welfare of others” “you don't think of your own pleasure” attachment lobha (attachment): akusala (unwholesome) “for the sake of one's own pleasant feeling” “we actually think of ourselves” “It is not a matter of should or should not. You are as you are.” “Unselfish love is characterised by considering the welfare of others. Attachment to other people is for the sake of one's own pleasant feeling.” The joys of life. Must a Buddhist give up music, dancing, books, laughing with friends and shopping? No. “We should live our daily life naturally, in order to understand our inclinations, our defilements. We should understand our attachment and aversion as they naturally arise. We can enjoy all the pleasant things but we should at the same time develop more understanding of the realities of our life.” The answer ends: “A wise person can live with pleasure and with understanding.” Small likes and dislikes. Like and dislike do not always lead to bad deeds23. Are they still unwholesome? Yes. “When it is of a lesser degree there is uneasiness or moodiness; we have no peace of mind. Whenever we have unpleasant feeling, the reality of aversion has arisen.” Why is ignorance unwholesome? “Ignorance conditions all defilements. There is ignorance with each unwholesome moment of consciousness24. Because of ignorance we live in darkness, we do not know what is wholesome and beneficial and what is unwholesome.” Ignorance also conditions wrong view25: “When we believe that body and mind can stay, that they are permanent, there is wrong view.” Happiness. How does one find happiness in Buddhism? “Through knowing realities as they are.” Why does that bring happiness? “Right understanding can eliminate26 ignorance and wrong view. Through right understanding there will be less clinging27, and that means more freedom.” How to begin. “One can read and consider what one reads and one should find the right person who can explain the teachings”. Heat. One question said that touching is already understood by everyone: “I know when I touch my ear or the chair. Everyone knows that. I know when I touch something which is hot.” The answer: “We say, for instance, that Cairo is hot or that a fire is hot. Heat itself is a reality which can be directly experienced through the bodysense28 without there being the need to name it. Heat is a reality which is true for everybody, it is absolute29 truth. When you think about Cairo or a fire you think long stories but there is no direct experience of a reality.” Tangible object. What can be experienced through the body? “Throughout the day we touch things which are hard. We believe that we touch a cup, plate or chair which are hard. In reality, it is hardness which is experienced through the bodysense, not a cup, plate or chair.” The full list: “Through bodysense the A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 52

Page 53

realities of hardness, softness, heat, cold, motion or pressure can be experienced. They are true for everybody, no matter how we name them.” “a cup, plate or chair”: concepts, known through memory what is directly experienced through the bodysense hardness softness heat cold motion pressure rūpa (matter): elements that arise because of conditions and fall away at once “They are true for everybody, no matter how we name them.” “Through bodysense the realities of hardness, softness, heat, cold, motion or pressure can be experienced.” Visible object. Is a car a visible object? “Visible object is that which seeing sees. It appears through eyesense. When we perceive30 a car we are already thinking of a concept, an idea.” Then the two kinds of reality: “Seeing is mental31, it experiences something. Visible object, that which is visible, is physical, it does not know anything. Hearing is mental, it experiences sound. Sound is physical, it does not know anything.” No self. The last questions were the hardest. How can anyone learn that there is no self? “The truth of non- self32 cannot be realized in the beginning. We have accumulated33 so much ignorance and wrong view. Through reading, considering and discussing there can gradually be more intellectual34 understanding of realities.” How can one be aware of realities? “There is seeing now. It can be realized that it is a reality which experiences visible object, just for a moment. It is not self which sees, seeing sees. You don’t have to do anything special in order to see.” What does it mean to understand seeing as “only a reality”? “One begins to understand that there is not my seeing which can stay on and which is so important.” Realities “are beyond control, they cannot arise because of anyone’s wish. Also awareness35 and understanding are realities which can only arise when there are the right conditions, they are beyond control. Beyond control is another way of saying that there is “only a reality”. The realities of our life are momentary36 and insignificant37. They arise and then disappear forever.” HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 2. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 3. concept: an idea put together by thinking, such as 'tree' or 'person'; it cannot be seen or touched by itself 4. verify: to check that something is true 5. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 6. vice: a bad habit 7. defilement: something that makes the mind dirty: wanting, anger, not knowing and the rest 8. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 9. beneficial: helpful; good for someone 10. skilful: done well, with skill; here, good for the mind (unskilful: bad for the mind) 11. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 12. inclination: a leaning towards something; what one tends to do A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 53

Page 54

13. rightful: allowed and proper; deserved 14. sane: of sound mind; sensible 15. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 16. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 17. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 18. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 19. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 20. unselfish: thinking of others, not of oneself 21. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 22. considerate: thinking of other people's feelings 23. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 24. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 25. wrong view: a wrong idea about what is real, such as the idea that there is a lasting self 26. eliminate: to get rid of 27. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 28. bodysense: the sense of touch, all over the body 29. absolute: complete and real in itself; not depending on names or ideas 30. perception: marking something in the mind so that it can be known again; remembering 31. mental: to do with the mind 32. non-self: not a self; not a person; not anyone's 33. accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it 34. intellectual: to do with thinking and understanding by the mind, not with seeing for oneself 35. awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness 36. momentary: lasting only a moment 37. insignificant: small and unimportant A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 54

Page 55

Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) The answers are at the back. 1. Where did Acharn Sujin’s talk with Ms Tuna take place? (a) in a papyrus shop (b) on a boat on the Bosporus (c) at Cairo airport (d) by the pyramids 2. What question did Acharn Sujin ask Ms Tuna about the soul and sleep? 3. “So, the soul has many functions in a day.” Which functions did Acharn Sujin list? (a) praying, fasting and giving (b) seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching and thinking (c) walking, running and sleeping (d) reading, writing and counting 4. Which word did Acharn Sujin prefer to “soul”, and why? (a) spirit, because it is older (b) consciousness, because soul implies something permanent (c) mind, because it is shorter (d) heart, because everyone has one 5. True or false: Acharn Sujin said that seeing belongs to a particular race or nationality. 6. Acharn Sujin compared becoming a good person to learning a skill. Which skill, and what did she say? 7. Which three defilements are the roots of unwholesome states of mind? (a) pride, envy and fear (b) attachment, aversion and ignorance (c) hunger, tiredness and pain (d) doubt, worry and sleepiness 8. True or false: the friends agreed that kings in history had rightful anger. 9. What is the difference between unselfish love and attachment, according to the interview? 10. Complete the sentence: “A wise person can live with … and with …” (a) silence; fasting (b) pleasure; understanding (c) books; teachers (d) patience; sleep 11. When a person touches a chair, what is directly experienced through the bodysense? (a) the chair (b) hardness (c) the idea of sitting (d) the colour of the chair A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 55

Page 56

12. Which realities can be experienced through the bodysense? 13. True or false: the interview says that through right understanding there will be less clinging, and that means more freedom. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 56

Page 57

Chapter 11: More questions in Egypt The three friends went on with their questions in Egypt. Nina’s last chapter is called “Further Interviews between Gabi, Alan and Nina in Egypt”. How should one live? “One should develop right understanding of the teachings by reading, considering and discussion. One should apply the teachings in one’s life as best as one can.” Is it selfish? Is a person who develops understanding only thinking about himself? “No, one develops more understanding of the world in and around oneself. The self is not a reality1. As understanding develops there will be less concern about the self.” When ignorance2 grows less, “there will be less unwholesomeness3 and this is beneficial4 for oneself and for the people around oneself.” “I do not feel that I have a great deal of ignorance.” One question said: “I know how to do my work, how to drive a car or how to cook.” The answer was that this is not the ignorance that matters: “We have ignorance of realities such as seeing, visible object5, hearing, sound, of all the realities which can be experienced6 through the five senses and through the mind-door. They appear only one at a time through one of the six doorways. They appear only for one moment and then they disappear. We are deluded7 about these fleeting8 realities and we take them for the world or the self.” eye door visible object ear door sound nose door odour tongue door flavour body door tangible object mind door all of these, and concepts six doorways, one object at a time “We mix up the six doorways and we join the different realities together” “They appear only one at a time through one of the six doorways.” “We mix up the six doorways and we join the different realities together instead of understanding realities as they are”. The six doorways are the eyes, the ears, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind. The answer ended with a question: “Would you like to understand that there is no self? Nothing belongs to you in reality.” Who decides? Is it not the self that makes the effort? “Intention9 is a mental10 reality; it arises11 when there are the appropriate conditions12. However, there is nobody who owns intention. It is the same with effort.” Meditation. “Do you apply yourself to meditation13?” The friends were careful with the word: “I avoid using the word meditation because different people have different ideas about it. Our goal should be the development of right understanding of the realities which appear now. We can begin to notice and consider one reality at a time and then there is no need to name it or to think about it. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 57

Page 58

Understanding can be developed in any situation, one does not have to change one’s life or do anything special.” This is called vipassanā (insight14), and “is a kind of mental development which can be done no matter where you are.” A quiet place? Is a quiet place not needed? “Not at all, because the purpose of the Buddha’s teachings is to understand the realities which arise naturally, in daily life.” “Sound is a reality, no matter where you are, whether it is quiet or whether there is a lot of noise. If we are in a noisy place and we have aversion15 towards that noise, aversion can be realized as just a conditioned16 reality, not “my aversion”.” “Sound is a reality, no matter where you are, whether it is quiet or whether there is a lot of noise.” How to begin. “Do you have to try now in order to see, to hear or to touch? These are realities which naturally arise in your life. When there are conditions for their arising, you cannot help but see, hear or touch.” And: “There is nobody who can force the arising of right understanding, it is conditioned by many factors.” Many people “just want to sit and concentrate17 on breathing, but they have to consider for themselves whether this is the way to know the realities of one’s daily life.” Understanding “can be accumulated18 little by little if one develops it naturally, without trying to make particular realities arise, without trying to control realities.” Results. A beginner wants to see some result19. “The result cannot be noticed immediately, it cannot be measured. However, as understanding develops there will be more confidence20.” And: “You will face unpleasant situations with more understanding and you will be more tolerant21 towards other people”. Dull? Is it not dull to study seeing and hearing? “If you just read about different realities it seems dull, but you should remember that they are the phenomena22 of your daily life. If you develop understanding of them when they appear, it is not boring but interesting.” Why study seeing and hardness at all? “We should A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 58

Page 59

come to understand that there is nobody who sees, nobody who hears, that there are only different conditioned realities.” A hidden virus. One of the three said that when he is seeing or hearing he has no idea of a self at all, so why must it be eradicated23? “We cannot say that there is an idea of self every time seeing or hearing arises. However, the idea of self is deeply accumulated. When it does not appear there is still the latent tendency24 of wrong view25. This is like a virus which is latent26 in the body but which can become active at any time.” Wrong view “can only be eradicated when enlightenment27 has been attained”, and it “must be eradicated first before attachment28 to sense objects can be eradicated”. Seeing and thinking. “It is important to have right understanding about seeing: it sees only what appears through the eyes, nothing else. When you pay attention to shape and form and when you perceive29 people and things there is remembrance30 of concepts31, there is thinking, not seeing. Seeing conditions thinking of concepts.” Would it be better not to think? “No. We should understand thinking as thinking, seeing as seeing, feeling as feeling; they are different realities.” A better person? “If there is more direct understanding of realities there will be less clinging32 to the idea of self. We shall think less of ourselves as a good person or a bad person.” Fatalism. If there is no self who can do anything, does nothing one does matter33? “There is no predestined34 fate35 ruling over our life. However, the different moments of our life are conditioned by the past and by the present.” A person who sees the value of understanding has “less inclination36 to laziness or to fatalism37“. Confidence. “We don’t have to wait for realities to appear as they are; we can still have confidence. There is confidence with each wholesome38 moment of consciousness39, for example, when we help someone else or when we study the teachings and consider them.” Backsliding. The ancient texts speak of monks40 who fell away from the teaching. When is a person backsliding41? “When one is no longer interested in developing understanding.” Does that happen when people are discouraged? “Even if it is difficult to develop understanding there are so many moments for you to start again. You can start again at every moment, whether you work or you don’t work, whether you are in a hurry or at leisure, it is the same. You always have an opportunity to start again. You may regret your lack of understanding, your forgetfulness, but what about this moment now?” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 59

Page 60

now at work start again now at leisure start again now in a hurry start again now tired start again now on a journey start again now at home start again every moment is a moment to begin “You may regret your lack of understanding, your forgetfulness, but what about this moment now?” “You can start again at every moment, whether you work or you don't work, whether you are in a hurry or at leisure, it is the same.” Work and free time. Is work more distracting? “There is no difference between your working situation and your free time.” “Our problems are caused by attachment, aversion and ignorance and these arise no matter where we are.” Wanting awareness. The last question of the book was Nina’s own problem from Chapter 7: wanting awareness42. Can a person tell himself not to want? The last answer: “When you understand that desire counteracts43 progress there will be conditions to stop wishing for results. Only intellectual44 understanding of the teachings, acquired by reading, considering and discussing can condition the arising of direct understanding, now or later on. There will be more patience when we remember that awareness and understanding do not belong to a self which can make them arise. Then, we can have the courage to begin again and again to find out more about the reality appearing at this moment.” HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 2. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 3. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 4. beneficial: helpful; good for someone 5. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 6. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 7. delusion: being fooled; not seeing things as they are 8. fleeting: passing very quickly 9. intention: what the mind means to do; the mind's choosing 10. mental: to do with the mind 11. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 12. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 13. meditation: developing the mind; people use this word in many different ways 14. insight: seeing into something; here, seeing clearly for oneself that there is only mind and matter 15. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 16. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 17. concentration: keeping the mind on one thing 18. accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it 19. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 20. confidence: trust in what is true and good; sureness 21. tolerant: putting up with things and people one does not like 22. phenomena: things that happen or appear; here, the realities of mind and matter A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 60
